utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have a decision to give. I'll give it. The Prosecution had asked to use an exhibit which is part of their second motion to amend the 65 ter exhibit list with confidential annex A filed confidentially on 18th August 2008. The Defence of Sredoje Lukic responded to this motion. Milan Lukic's Defence has not yet responded. However, the motion concerns a request for the admission of nine exhibits to the Prosecution's exhibit list. Proposed exhibits 6 to 9 are number 6, a map depicting the area between Visegrad and Rogatica; 7, a map book; and 8, a 360-degree photograph presentation; and the ninth is a photograph book. The Trial Chamber will allow the Prosecution to add these four exhibits to their exhibit list and will render a written decision on the remaining five exhibits once the Milan Lukic Defence has responded to the motion. The dead-line for this response is September 1, 2008. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it has been suggested I tell you that the first break would be at 9.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you are to continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Madam.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Have you had a bit of a rest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a bit. Thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I introduce myself. I am Djuro Cepic, and I am Defence counsel for Sredoje Lukic, I am one of his lawyers and I am going to put a few questions to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please listen to my questions carefully and give clear answers as briefly as possible so that we would go through my questions as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, you told me that while you were working, that is how I understood your testimony in relation to the period that you were explaining, on workdays you worked at the factory doing a certain job. Could you tell us what you did on non-working days, that is to say, Saturdays and Sundays, when you did not go to work. What were your activities, very briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? Has the interpretation finished? May I answer? On Saturday and Sunday I worked at the company quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically about these activities outside work. This is my very precise question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took care of my daughter, and for the most part I was at the apartment and I went to the family house and I went to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear the end of the sentence, please. The interpreter did not hear. You are overlapping, Mr. Cepic, and the witness, so the interpreter is having a problem. You said: "I went to the family house and to the ..." and it was cut off there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying that my work obligation was on Saturday and Sunday, that I had very little free time because there were war operations in the town of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the witness's statement again; Mr. Cepic spoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you are coming in too quickly. You speak the same language so there is a natural tendency to overlap. Let us have the end of your sentence. You said you had very little free time because there were war operations in the town of Visegrad. Did you say anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I repeated that in the town of Visegrad there were war operations so I could not be in these war operations. My work obligation was to do my job at the company, sometimes even on Saturdays and Sundays, until 10.00 or 12.00 because the kitchen was a big one at the company and then the military also came for breakfast and lunch there and that's where they slept, and this was on our work premises. So my work obligation was on a daily basis and day and night at that. I did not have too much free time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, I'm going to go back to part of your testimony. On the 27th of August on page 78 of the transcript you explained that it was a workday and that you were returning from work when you saw a lot of soldiers forcing people up Pionirska Street. Could you please tell me how long you worked on that day, tentatively, until what time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I read this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, you may not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, all right, but I can't remember that it was the 27th of August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that you want to read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to read what it was that I wrote, what I wanted to make by way of a statement on that day, because as for dates I didn't remember them very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, do you attach a lot of importance to this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would like to clarify just some things very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because she wanted to read something. You have a document there? What is the document that you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. What I meant was that I read it from the screen. He mentioned the 27th of August, so if I -- well, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see, reading it from the screen. Of course you can read it from the screen. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I am going to put to you what it was that you said on the 27th of August, that is to say, the day before yesterday. Two days ago, you said in relation to the incident in Pionirska Street --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see, oh, oh, the 27th of August, I'm so sorry. I thought that this was many years ago. I didn't realize.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to clarify everything. So the transcript page was 78. In relation to the incident in Pionirska you explained to us that this was in mid-June 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You were going back from work, it was a workday, and you saw many soldiers forcing people ahead in Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What I would be interested in is hearing approximately how long you were at work on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, it's been 18 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for me --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Can you just say briefly: I remember, I do not remember, or roughly when it might have happened so that we would go through this quickly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. It could have been four or five hours in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How was it that you got home from work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the centre of town, I don't remember. I assume that someone drove me in a vehicle. Further on to both apartments, I went on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Since it was a workday, what did other employees do? How did they go home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part we used transportation vehicles, or rather, a small bus that went through the centre of town and that drove further on to the surrounding villages. Even if I would take the bus I would have to get off in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I may assume, it's the month of June, it must have been sunny, warm, short sleeves. What kind of clothes did people wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was a real summer day, then of course it would be short sleeves; but if it would rain, again, short sleeves wouldn't bother you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember what the weather was like -- oh, let me wait for them to interpret this. Do you remember perhaps what the weather was like? This was mid-June, as you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it may have rained in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was it like in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It's been a long, long time. It's been a long time. I do not remember. How could I remember exactly now? How can I give you a precise record of what it was like, warm, rainy, whatever? I can't remember, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about the morning, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it rained, but even that I do not remember with 100 per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to the incident in Bikavac. Yesterday you said to us that this happened in the afternoon when you came across Milan Lukic and his group. Would you tell me whether on that day you went directly to Bikavac from work or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. This was in the early evening, just before the evening, not directly from work. That is to say, first I'd have to stop and carry out my obligations in order to do what I had to do. If somebody would give me a phone call, like those two old people, I could not go straight from work, for instance, because Bikavac is pretty far away from the centre of town too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What time was it roughly, do you remember? It was day-time, I assume, as long as you mentioned the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after my working hours, in the afternoon. If I worked until 4.00 or 5.00, it was in the afternoon. But I repeat, you never knew how long I would stay at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Of course. On the day when the incident occurred, was that a workday as well? How did the other workers go back home, do you remember perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a few moments ago, all the workers used a transportation vehicle; I used the company car more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. What about this particular day, work day or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But you said you spent that day working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that really tells you the story, doesn't it. I can't remember whether I was working on that day or not. It was a matter of my work obligation and that included the weekends. Please don't forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You said this was in broad daylight, it wasn't night-time. You said you got off work at about 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon. What time would that be? It gets dark at about 8.00, so what time would this have been that you saw Milan Lukic's group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime close to that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was just before the curfew, before 8.00 that evening. There was still sufficient daylight outside. It hadn't gotten dark yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So that would mean, roughly speaking, before 7.00 p.m., wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite remember. I had a horrendous headache yesterday. It's very difficult for me to focus today. I apologise. I'm certain it was before nightfall because there was plenty of daylight still outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system Exhibit number P32, please. Thank you. That's quite fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, here's the map that you drew yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I must have gotten something wrong here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you please do this for us, use a different colour now to draw something for us on this map and could we have Ms. Usher's assistance for this. Could you mark the main road, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'd like a thin pen or pencil for that. I was using a felt pen yesterday which was actually quite unwieldy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is this the road that takes us from that hilltop down towards the centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Cepic, what is it you wanted me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The main route from the centre on to Bikavac and then right around your homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, the main road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you see what I'm pointing at?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Not quite yet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you can't. All right. Perhaps I should just stand up. This is the main road that takes you from the centre. All of this, the main road as far as -- as far as Banpolje, this is the main road, all of this, the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you look at the main road can you please do this for us now, Banpolje, near Banpolje --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, I understand this is under seal so we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Oh, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, but just draw an arrow in that general direction.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the main road you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Towards the very bottom of the map or the image. This is near Megdan. Can we see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The letter C, please, mark it there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this good enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D17, page 12, the same page number applies both to the B/C/S and the English. [In English] Before we change exhibit on our screens could we have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit 2D2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have now in e-court system or a little bit later on we will return back on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you provided a physical description of my client, Sredoje Lukic. You specified that he was wearing some sort of a sock, a mask, on his head and he did this in order not to be recognised by Visegrad's inhabitants, or at least that's what you said. You said that he had this pulled over his head in both of the incidents involved. You will agree with me that in that case one could not actually see his hair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when he wore the sock one could not see his hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Or the eyes for that matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, the eyes -- one could see his eyes. How else would a man -

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but underneath that, you couldn't recognise...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man had - had his eyes open...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. But since he had this mask or sock pulled over his head, then probably there was nothing really to distinguish him in terms of specific features, something that would reveal Sredoje Lukic's identity to anyone else -

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew Sredoje -

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not talking about you, I'm talking about other people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Other people could not possibly have identified him since he had this sock or mask, though he was wearing a uniform too, just like other people, but there were no distinguishing features that would set him apart from anybody else, were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose there were a lot of people who recognised him even with the sock by the sound of his voice because all residents of Visegrad knew Sredoje. The man had his eyes open. At the time -

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be fair to say that at the time during the Bikavac incident and the Pionirska Street incident you were in a state of shock, you were just imagining Sredoje Lukic, you wanted to see him there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not that I was assuming he would be there or that I thought I would see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 1D18, please, page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this comes up, that's your 2000 statement to the investigators, Madam, and then we'll be going back to Bikavac briefly. Could you please read paragraph 2 for me, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left or on the right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: On the left, the B/C/S. Could you read it out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A week after the Pionirska Street incident --" is this fine?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A week after the Pionirska Street incident, a similar incident happened in an area of town called Bikavac. About 70 people, men, women, children, and elderly people, were forced into Meho and Dervisa Aljic's house. (redacted) I was on the main road when this happened. They ordered them to enter the ground floor of that house. When I say 'they,' I mean the members of Milan Lukic's gang. I was scared and I started walking back towards the centre of town ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have again on our screens 2D2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, this is your statement, your 2000 statement, isn't it? We discussed this, haven't we? Yesterday during your evidence you said something that does not tally with what your statement reflects. You said you weren't coming back from the actual town, but rather you were coming from the direction of your home when you came across Milan Lukic's group. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Unlike your evidence yesterday, in your statement you claim that you were standing on the main road -- Madam, you said yesterday that you were in this orchard and that (redacted) Nonetheless, in your 2000 statement, which was a sworn statement and you took three days to make --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please just allow me to finish. You said something that seems to be quite the opposite of this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You claim in your statement that you were standing on the main road, but then you got scared and you headed back towards the centre of town. My question to you, Madam: Does there not seem to be quite a notable difference between the two, a discrepancy, if you like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I tell you about my reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just say yes or no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, if she has a reason she's entitled to give it and I certainly would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the genocide at Bikavac, the evidence came for the first time this year. I never testified about this. I'm only talking about it now. Back in 2001 I wasn't talking about Bikavac. That was the short version of my evidence, and Bikavac was never mentioned during the Vasiljevic case. Back at the time, Mr. Cepic, I was quite afraid during my evidence because Mr. Lukic, both of them, in fact, were still at large. So please, try not to cause any serious health problems for me. There you have my answer. I'm not here to be scared or intimidated by you. I'm not here for you to pose a threat to my health. I am here to give evidence to the best of my recollection and ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you see the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, two days ago you testified about the incident at Pionirska Street. You said that two ladies who witnessed the incident survived. Why did you call them witnesses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that two persons survived the massacre. When I said "witnesses" I meant survivors.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, did you have occasion to see the Mitar Vasiljevic judgement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The final judgement? No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Doesn't it sound a bit strange that in your testimony during the direct examination you omitted the parts about which you were discredited in that judgement until my colleague Alarid did not take you back to that story concerning two Mitar Vasiljevics, the older and the younger one, doesn't that sound a bit strange to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did mention the older and the younger Mitar Vasiljevic at the same trial too, and then I carried out this identification by way of photograph; that is to say, when I was shown a photograph then I made a distinction between the two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why did you refuse to grant an interview to our Defence team in the pre-trial stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We informed our colleagues from the OTP that we wished to speak to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, by phone?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, we filed a request to the effect that we wished to speak to you. Our colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor said that you refused to talk to us in any way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not refusing. Please go ahead. Here I am. I'll give you all the answers I can give. Yesterday, I do apologise, there was a lot of tension involved and I had to concentrate a great deal, if you really want to be fair about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, I believe my colleagues from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe them and I believe you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This was two months ago. You refused to talk to our Defence team, and I'm asking you why.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, can I explain it now, how this happened? Now you are saying that I refused. I was at work. I could not talk. You found me when I was at work. A question was put to me, Madam, do you want to talk to the Lukic/Lukic lawyers? Do you want to talk to them? And then after that conversation you can withdraw. And I said, No, no, out of fear, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Why did you refuse to talk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without thinking at all any more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have admission of this exhibit on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit Number 2D3 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I forgot to say that it has to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We mentioned VG-114, or rather, you mentioned VG-114?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You believe that she is a credible person and that she could provide the most relevant information about the incident at Bikavac, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You would believe her, you would believe her words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Then, Madam, you are not telling the truth. You said that it was daylight and that one could see and VG-114 says in her statement that it's 9.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 9.00 in the evening when I could not longer be present because it was curfew time by then --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Madam, would you believe me if I were to say to you that you are not telling the truth even about the incident in Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling the truth and I am sorry that I could not talk to you on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please, may I finish my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You said that it was a workday. You described to us how it was that you were getting back from work --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I said roughly, roughly, a workday, every day was a workday. All right. I agree with you that I said that it was a workday. Please go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You were explicit about this. You described to us how other workers went home on that day and how you came home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that it was 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, reference, your transcript, your testimony, page 78, the 27th of August, 2008, lines 18 through 23 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you believe me that the Trial Chamber ascertained that this was a holiday, a religious holiday in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would sometimes go on working throughout the religious festivities, but I do believe what you're telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thirdly and lastly, are you aware of the fact that in the Vasiljevic case the Trial Chamber found you to be a witness that was not credible or reliable. This is in 89 -- paragraphs 89, 90, and 150 [as interpreted] of the judgement and perhaps other references too.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Cepic, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Paragraphs 89, 90, and 159 from Vasiljevic judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Ossogo, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Your Honour, on the issue of people whom VG-115 has seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: VG 115, I would like you to look around the courtroom, take you time, and let me know and tell the Bench whom you recognise with the exception of myself, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think that is not something which was raised from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, we are not with you on this one because it seems to us that the whole question of identity has been a principal plank of the cross-examination. Go ahead, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can identify both Milan and Sredoje Lukic in this courtroom, and if I may just apologise to Mr. Cepic for not having been able to talk to him on the phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that some people had put their hands in front of their face. I wanted to make sure that these people could be properly identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but let her tell us which Cepic is which Cepic -- sorry, which Lukic is which Lukic. I'm very sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to add something, there are plenty of Cepic lawyers, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say this now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milan Lukic, wearing a black suit; next to him, Mr. Sredoje Lukic, who used to be bald and wear a sock over his head but now he has plenty of hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness VG-115. And those are the two people you saw on Pionirska Street the day the incident took place? When this person's house burnt down, these are the two men you saw; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was much surprised about Milan Lukic because I think he's changed a lot. It's probably his age, must have left a trace. Sredoje hasn't changed that much actually. I used to know Sredoje from before. I only got to know Milan Lukic during the war, but I used to know Sredoje while he still worked as a police officer and as I said yesterday he was a person whom I felt a great deal of affection for. When the war first started, Sredoje would walk around with his head shaved entirely. He didn't have any hair to speak of. Why was he using the sock? I suppose only he could tell us that. Milan Lukic was a man of striking looks, always very neat, very orderly, closely cropped, always clean and neat and he always stood out in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness VG-115. So you can confirm that these are the two people you saw on Pionirska Street who were monitoring the civilians you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that I saw them at Pionirska Street and Sredoje was standing in my nearest proximity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. And these two people you -- whom you have identified, Milan Lukic wearing a dark suit and Sredoje Lukic, are the two men you saw in Bikavac when this incident took place and which you described at length during your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I would like just request opportunity to ask some additional questions of this witness. I think some topics are raised right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but are you saying they didn't arise out of cross-examination because you've had your turn. The only way that I would allow --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- the only way I would allow you to ask additional questions is if I have allowed the Prosecutor to re-examine exceptionally on a matter that didn't arise. And sometimes I do do that, but I'm not aware that that has happened here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With your leave, page 26, line 25 and page 27, line 1, she confirmed that she was standing in the nearest proximity of my client; I didn't hear that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let the Prosecutor finish his re-examination and then we'll consider your submission. And when we come to consider it, I'll ask the Prosecutor to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I shall continue by asking you this question: VG-115, are these the two people who you saw during that incident in Bikavac when these two men did what you stated in your prior statement, i.e., forcing these civilians to go into Mr. Aljic's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw these two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Witness VG-115, you told us that the reason why you testify in this case, it is because you wanted justice to prevail and this is why you have accepted to come and testify here before this Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-115 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely. I'm here to testify for the sake of justice and not because the gentleman offended me yesterday with his racist remark, saying that I was emanating hatred for the Serbs. I don't think he should ever have allowed himself to say anything like that. The only reason I'm here is to tell the truth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Witness. You're saying that yesterday you were offended by a gentleman with his racist remark. Speaking for myself, I -- I don't know that any racist remarks were uttered in this court. I would not have allowed that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me that I was teeming with hatred against the Serbs, and that was a bit rich because I'm a Serb myself. The only reason I'm here is to tell the truth and to say what those who died then and who are still alive went through at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on. Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness VG-115.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us now deal with the submission by Mr. Cepic that -- Mr. Ossogo, Mr. Cepic submitted that in your re-examination for the first time there was a mention by this witness that she saw his client, Sredoje, on Pionirska Street. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has always stated that Milan and Sredoje Lukic were in -- the main perpetrators together with associates and were involved in those facts that occurred in Pionirska. I don't think she made up this new fact. As far as the two incidents are concerned, the burning down of the house on Pionirska Street and the Bikavac incident, well, these are two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is a matter, of course, that can be checked, but you would be in the best position to tell us. In your examination-in-chief, did you lead any evidence from her that she saw Sredoje on Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I don't have the exact line on the transcript that I can say -- if we look at page 701, lines 24 to 25 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: In today 's transcript or yesterday's transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript dated the 27th -- 28th, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Legal Officer will check this for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we have here does not mention any page number so I can't check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you give us the reference again, Mr. Ossogo?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 701, lines 24 to 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: On the transcript we have of the 28th the page numbering starts with page 1, so if you could indicate the page number on the document that we're all looking at that could help. [Interpretation] But the -- what Mr. Cepic was saying, that the witness was standing close to Sredoje Lukic, I haven't seen that on the transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add one thing? I would like to say something about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, we'll come to you when we're ready, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I can read it out. I don't actually have the page on my screen. I shall read it out in English. [In English] "They were standing on this very narrow road in front of me ... "I could recognise the members of their group because I had come to know them very well when they came to my enterprise. Among them there were also citizens of Visegrad." [Interpretation] The witness continues. [In English] "I shall do my best to remember them all. Milan Lukic was there, Sredoje Lukic, so Milan Lukic with his father, Mile ..." That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that raises the question, Mr. Cepic, it was raised in examination-in-chief and you would have had therefore an opportunity to contest that allegation in your cross-examination, and therefore I would not allow you to do so now, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness -- are you sitting as if you want to rise, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I think that the witness was more specified during the re-direct examination and she said -- specifically for Sredoje Lukic she said something about his hair which is not mentioned in the direct examination, about his description. So for me this is a new topic and she gave more specific information related to incident on 28th page, line -- line 2 and 3, that two of them forcing these civilians into the house of Aljic. So she could see those two persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. I maintain the decision that I made. Witness, that concludes your evidence, we thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution calls VG-104, Mirsada Kahriman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, and you may sit. You may begin, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Kahriman.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could you please kindly state your full name and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Kahriman Mirsada; the 15th of September, 1962; Visegrad, Dusce.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, in the spring of 1992, in what village did you live?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Dusce.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And in what municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the information of the Court, Ms. Kahriman is a 92 ter witness so I'll be proceeding to have her confirm her prior statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, did you give a statement to ICTY investigators on the 14th of March, 2001?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review that statement in the Bosnian language before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When we met earlier this week, we discussed several clarifications to that original statement and you provided an additional statement to ICTY investigators and myself this week. Do you recall giving that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was that statement read back to you in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Before I ask you to confirm both those prior statements, there's one additional clarification. When you were interviewed by ICTY investigators in March of 2001, were you shown any pages containing photographs?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, there were some photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many pages, how many pieces of paper, with photographs, you were shown?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: There was a single page with photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If I were to ask you today the same questions you were asked in your two prior statements, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honours, pursuant to Rule 92 ter I tender into evidence Ms. Kahriman's two ICTY statements. The first is dated the 14th of March, 2001, which is 65 ter number 172; the second is dated 26th of August, 2008, it does not have a 65 ter number, but the ERN is 0638-2685 to 0638-2689.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 172 will become Exhibit P33 -- 34; and ERN 0638-2685 will become Exhibit P35.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, I'm going to ask you just a few additional questions. In your statement you discuss numerous occasions between the 18th of May, 1992, and the 14th of June, 1992, when you eye-witnessed Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic committing crimes in Visegrad. I'm going to ask you now a few questions about your knowledge of Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic. In your 14th of March, 2001, ICTY statement you describe the first time you met Milan Lukic and he introduced himself to you. Can you recall what he said to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He told me at the Drina bridge that his name was Milan Lukic, he was 25, and he was there to cut some Muslim throats.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was that he said this to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you know Milan Lukic before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe Milan Lukic as he looked when he introduced himself to you and spoke those words?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Milan Lukic was wearing a military uniform with insignia showing two white eagles, it was an armband on his sleeve. Hair neither long nor short, sort of medium, and he never wore any caps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, we are going to take the break now, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, before we took the break we were discussing how you knew Milan Lukic. To your knowledge was there anyone else by the name of Milan Lukic in Visegrad during 1992 other than the man that you have just described?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you a few questions about Sredoje Lukic. In your statement you speak about Sredoje Lukic. Did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, I knew him because I saw him but I didn't have any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Before the war, how frequently would you say you saw Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, I saw him before the war two or three times a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In your ICTY statements which are now in evidence you describe events which you eye-witnessed which took place at your next-door neighbour's house on the 18th of May, 1992. These events relate to acts you eye-witnessed in which Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic stole your neighbour Behija Zukic's cherry red Passat and their truck, abducted six men and boys, and killed Behija Zukic. I would like to ask you just a few questions in relation to these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the leading nature of the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a 92 ter witness. The statements are in evidence. This is merely a summary to put the witness's -- put the questions that I'm going to put to the witness in context. These are merely additional questions to add on to her information which is already in evidence through these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What is the approximate distance between your house and the Zukic house?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: -- metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was the interpretation cut off? Could you please kindly repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: 2 metres, there were 2 metres between my house and Behka's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In your statements you describe three times on the 18th of May, 1992, when Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic came to the Zukic home. Can you estimate the distance between where you were standing and the events you describe during the first visit to the Zukic home.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The first time they came, again it was 2 metres away, when Milan Lukic returned Behka -- and Sredoje Lukic too, when they returned them from town to their house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: On the second time Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic came to the Zukic home that day, how close was your observation point to those events?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps it was a metre away when Milan Lukic came the other time and took people away on a truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: On the third visit when you say in your statement that Ms. Zukic was shot and killed, how close were you to Milan Lukic when you observed Behija Zukic's body?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I crossed my terrace to Faruk's room and I saw Behka's body lying in the hall, part of it in the hall, part of it in the living-room.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Faruk. Can you tell the Court, please, who Faruk is.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Faruk is Behka's son.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How close were you to Milan Lukic when you observed Behka -- Behija Zukic's body?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Maybe I was a metre away when Milan killed Behka and when he said that I would be the next victim.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How close were you to Sredoje Lukic when you observed Behija Zukic's body?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Sredoje Lukic was a bit further away from Milan Lukic. I cannot tell you now exactly how big the distance was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you see Milan Lukic carrying anything or holding anything at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He was holding an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you see Sredoje Lukic carrying anything or holding anything at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He had a rifle on his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: During these events how was Milan Lukic dressed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He was wearing military clothing, and he had an emblem of the White Eagles that was sewn on to his sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And how was Sredoje Lukic dressed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Just like Milan Lukic, they were dressed the same way, the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind as to what you say in your statement, that Milan Lukic stole Behija Zukic's cherry red Passat?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He personally stole Behija's Passat.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind as to what you say in your statement, that Sredoje Lukic drove the truck that carried away the six men and boys from the Zukic home?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No doubt in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind as to what you say in your statement, that Milan Lukic shot Behija Zukic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Milan Lukic did not shoot Behija Zukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, the Trial Chamber is of the view that the better procedure for you to adopt is to summarize the -- to have the witness herself give a summary of the points which you wish to elicit from her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just to clarify, with regard to 92 ter witnesses because of the limitation of time it was our understanding that the procedure is that we admit the -- her confirmation of the prior statements and then seek certain clarifications on particular points. In order to focus the witness on those particular points, the questions are put in this very specific way, and that was the purpose especially because in an identification case there are necessarily certain questions which must be asked in court and that lengthens the time in chief. So this was the last question which -- with regard to the Zukic incident. After that I was going to discuss some sightings of the accused and then conclude. Are you asking me to put -- to ask the witness in detail about the incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not at all, not at all; it's the exact opposite. The point I'm making is that the evidence should come from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And not from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. Understood, understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So before we -- before I ask you one last question about the Zukic incident, I'd like to clarify your last response. I believe there may have been a translation problem. You said earlier in your testimony here, and as well in your statements, that Milan Lukic had killed Behija Zukic. Now I asked you the question of whether there's any doubt in your mind of that fact that you testified to, and I think the translation -- I think you said "nije," which means no, and I'd like to ask you to please repeat that answer, whether no, he didn't shoot her, or no, you don't doubt it. So I ask you one more time to be clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, there are too many leading questions here. That's what we're hearing from the Prosecutor. That is the only thing I wish to point out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Prosecutor is asking her to clarify her last response, so that's already in evidence. Yes, give the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, did you understand the question or would you like me to repeat that last question?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I understood the question. Milan Lukic killed Behka Zukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, between the 10th of June, 1992, when your husband was unfortunately killed, and the 14th of June, 1992, how many times would you estimate you crossed the old Visegrad bridge?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I'd cross the old Visegrad bridge six times a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: For clarification purposes, when you say "six times a day," is that six times crossing in one direction or six round trips?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: It's six times going there and back, that is to say that I would cross the bridge three times a day going there and back.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Why were you crossing the bridge so frequently between the 10th of June and the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I went to try to bury my husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How many times during those four days did you see Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Every time I crossed the bridge I saw Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic, I saw them at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How many times during those four days did you see Behija Zukic's red Passat?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The number of times I saw Milan Lukic, that's the number of times I saw the Passat at the bridge, it was always parked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How was Milan Lukic dressed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He wore military clothing, and on his sleeve he had the emblem of the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How was Sredoje Lukic dressed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Just like Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, I'd like to ask you to look around the courtroom and please tell us if you recognise anyone in the courtroom here today apart from myself. Please take your time and be sure that you, in fact, do recognise someone, if you do, before you speak.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I do not recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, can you tell the Court how did the crimes that you witnessed affect you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I've already said that Behka Zukic was killed, that people were taken away, I've already said that, all of that is in my statement. They killed my husband and that's in the record, who it was that killed him. Milan and Sredoje Lukic from the 10th of June, 1992, that is when it was the Muslim holiday of Kurban Bajram and that is when they killed the largest number of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, with your indulgence may I ask one last follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, can you tell the Court when was the last time you saw Milan or Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The last time I saw Milan was on the 14th of June, 1992, in front of the Visegrad Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And the last time that you saw Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's when I saw him, on that same day, but they were apart.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you see any of them in court today, either Milan or Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today they're both here but I cannot recognise them. It's been 16 years, that's a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am. My name is Jason Alarid. Just in terms of the statements you've given in these proceedings, I'm looking at the interpreter certificates and I note that the statements were read to you. So is it fair to say that you do not read and write the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I know how to read and write in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you read your -- because I was merely referring to what the interpreter certificate said is that the statements were read to you by an interpreter, and so it appeared that you did not read them yourself before you signed them.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I read them personally and I signed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, do you realize -- or rather, did you also read a statement in preparation for this that was given in June -- excuse me, July 23rd, 1992, in which your signature appears on the last page?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I read the statement, there is no need for me to read it when I know it off by heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, ma'am, this statement was -- had on the cover sheet the -- that it was given to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Security Services Centre, the 23rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I did make a statement. I made a statement to the journalist about security, no one else but the journalist. It was a handwritten statement. It wasn't written on a computer or on a printing machine. It is my signature and what is written there is even more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What is written is more than the statement you wrote in handwriting or more than you told who you call now a journalist back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness did not say that she wrote the statement; the witness simply said it was a handwritten statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I guess then the question -- I was confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you actually write a handwritten statement of which you turned over to this journalist, as you say; or did the journalist make a handwritten statement of which you saw?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The journalist wrote it personally in his own hand. I did not write that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But regardless, you do identify your signature at the end of the Serbian typewritten statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we have and I would tender it as evidence 1D00-3146, which is an English translation of a witness statement of Mirsada Kahriman given 23rd July 1992, with the caveats of the witness, of course; and the signed statement is 1D00-3177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement will become Exhibit number 1D23.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I submit that before the learned counsel puts questions to the witness on this, that there are apparently some questions about the authenticity of this document and that he should lay a foundation first that it is, in fact, the witness's statement. She's presented some confusion about whether she in fact gave a statement to the police. She said that she signed a handwritten statement, whereas this statement is typewritten and she said she gave a statement to the journalist, whereas this statement appears on police letterhead. So I submit, especially in light of paragraphs 2 and 3 of the witness's statement from the 26th of August, that there are some questions that have to be asked first before detailed questions are put on this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just -- as part of the 65 ter disclosures we have actually only received an unsigned typewritten statement and we received the signed statement of which this witness refers to as an authentic signature just this week and so that is when we uploaded it into the e-court as our 1D00-31 -- excuse me, 3177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, ask the questions necessary to clarify the matter. And of course, Ms. Marcus, you will have an opportunity to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, second statement 1D00-3177 will become 1D24.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And could we on side by side have the English version and the Serbian or B/C/S signed version, please, and we can start at page 1 for foundational purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, can you just simply read the first sentence of the first page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: "Record. "Citizen Mirsada Kahriman, daughter of Sahin Dragulj and mother Hatema, nee Ramic, born the 15th of September, 1962, in the village of Draguljevici, Rogatica municipality, completed primary school, housewife, married, mother of two ..." Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, please, just the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: " ... permanently residing at the hamlet of Dusce number 74, Visegrad municipality, husband Ekrem killed by the Chetniks in the village of Osojnica, pursuant to Article 151 of the Law on Criminal Procedure made the following ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, is that personal information about you true to the --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, all of this information is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that the person that generated this statement had to have spoken with you to get this personal information with specificity?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: A journalist talked to me, it was no investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So he specifically identified him as a journalist? For what news organization?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Oh, well, there's one thing I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would the witness require us to go into private session to reveal what you can't say in open court?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The -- counsel asked a compound question and witness answered only one. I'm not sure it was clear which question she was answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's possible that that's a clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, breaking the question up, the person did identify him as a journalist; is that what you're saying today?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: As a journalist, and I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so nothing to add is you're not aware of what news agency or organization this journalist worked for?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I don't know about the agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But let's just go through what this journalist may have generated and see if some of these facts are true or not; does that sound fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that your memory of events related to the summer of 1992 were fresher in your mind in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, you stated on direct examination that you have difficulty recognising the gentlemen in the courtroom because 16 years have passed; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It's difficult because they killed half my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And "they," are you specifically referring to the gentlemen in the courtroom today or are you just referring to "they" as Serbians in general?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just one correction in transcript with your leave, page 48, line 5, I think the witness answered "hamam." She used the word "hamam."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Meaning what? Interpreter, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That "hamam" killed them or something in that sense. "Hamam," it means something like -- I just hear interpretation not in Serbian, it is in Bosnian, it means something like possibly or -- it's Arabian word, it's not Serbian or Bosnian word, actually. So if we have more clarification about that issue, I think it would be useful. Thank you very much. I do apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the word used nor do we understand Arabic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me go back then to the witness. Witness, you were asked -- you were reminded that in direct examination you said you had difficulty recognising the gentlemen in the courtroom because 16 years had passed, and counsel asked you: "Isn't that true?" And the answer which have on the transcript is: "Yes. It's difficult because they killed half my family." Was that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, ma'am, what do you mean by the word "hamam"?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: "Aman," "aman," it's a Turkish word. It means, if I try to give you all the names I don't think 20 volumes would be sufficient to give all their names, how many people they killed and how many people they wronged and how much evil they caused, Milan and Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What is -- would be your definition of the word "aman," the Turkish word?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: "Aman," this is a Turkish word. Many people were involved, it wasn't just them, and killed Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you spoke in terms of generally the Serbians killing half your family as opposed to specifically the gentlemen in this courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Those two as well caused a lot of harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But in fact you had specific information that other people had -- identified had killed your husband in fact?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Other people, the man's name is Slobodan Tripkovic and he lives at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you just repeat the last part of your answer, Witness, the interpreter did not get it. Where does Slobodan live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Visegrad at Okoliste.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: He lives there today?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When did he live there, as far as your recollection allows you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Since he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when was the last time you had information of his whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The last time I saw him was in 2002 and he was still at Okoliste.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so he lived with impunity after supposedly killing your husband in the town of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He has not been punished or even arrested yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he wasn't charged with being a member of the White Eagles as you knew him to be?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, I can't say. He was with the White Eagles. He was killing Muslims, so he must have belonged to some army or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I would like to go back to the first page of the statement and right below the term "statement" there are some facts that I would like you to either agree or disagree with. Would you agree that the SDS and Serbian Democratic Party extremists from Visegrad and the surroundings were saying that Serbia -- or excuse me, Visegrad was going to be the Greater Serbia before the fighting even started?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: That was a long time ago. They said there wouldn't be a war and then they sang songs to the effect that they would create Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you heard this and that would have been something you would have given to this interviewer?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I personally heard them saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this would have been information that you would have passed on to investigating persons investigating the death of your husband as well as the violence in Visegrad; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you would have -- and is it true that officials of the SDS party were carrying a Chetnik flag with skulls on it at the time; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you knew some of those officials by sight. Can you name them?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, Veselin Vucelja, and then I can't remember the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And are you saying you knew as officials of the SDS prior to the fighting starting in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I didn't know if they were from that or not. It was only after the war had begun that I learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And nowhere in any of these statements are you saying that you saw any of these gentlemen with the black flag with the skull on it; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I saw Milan Lukic carrying a black flag with a skull.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now after those -- isn't it true that you saw one of the members of the SDS tell the people in the square that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I may be mistaken but I believe there was something omitted from the translation of the last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: She said: "I saw Milan Lukic carrying a black flag with a skull," and then she mentions a name. What did you say after that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said Milan Lukic was carrying that flag in Behka's Passat as well, personally. It was in some car before and then it was on Behka's car that he put that flag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How was it mounted to the Passat, the flag?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, I can't say. I can't explain. You have to ask the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you. You said you saw it. Is it on the front? Is it on the back? Is it on top? How was it attached?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Mostly it was inside, on the inside of the door. I can't remember it, if it was the driver's door or not. For the most part not because it was him who drove, it had to be the back seat door and sometimes they would hold it in their hands.
