utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Before the fighting, is it true that an official of the SDS told dozens of people in -- publicly in the town of Visegrad that Greater Serbia would be formed in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this caused insecurity between -- to be spread amongst the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: We trusted everyone. We thought the war would never happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But don't -- isn't it true that such nationalistic talk amongst the SDS would cause fear and insecurity amongst the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, ma'am, were these officials of the SDS Risto Perisic, do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Risto Perisic, yes, I know, but I can't say who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about Branimir Savovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I don't know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about Veselin Vucelja?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Veselin Vucelja was over at Bikavac. What was he, he wore the same clothes as they. How should I know? He worked with some service of theirs or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And yet, in your first statement of the 14th of March, 2001, you considered Mr. Vucelja the leader of the White Eagles; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the answer is yes, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in the statement to the purported journalist, there is information that propaganda was being published to the Serbians and Muslims alike, of course, that Serbians were being exterminated in Visegrad; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Serbs were moving out of their own accord; no one was exterminating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yet they were fearful because of what they were hearing on the news and the radio?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this witness has any basis for explaining how the Serbs in town felt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will hear her answer. Are you able to answer that question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, move on, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it -- do you know if the Serbians were hearing that Serbian children were being roasted on spits?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know if they were -- heard that they were being -- Serbian women were being shod like horses?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were Serbians hearing that other Serbians were being forced from their homes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I'm going to stop you. I don't believe she can really say what Serbians were hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it true that in March of 1992 you were working at the Terpentin family -- factory, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you had a colleague named Mara, who was a Serbian, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And she told you that she was afraid that the Green Berets would slaughter them and she, in fact, left her job; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: She left herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did she tell you that -- did you tell her that it was not true that the Green Berets were slaughtering Serbians?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did she tell you that, You'll see when our Serbs come to slaughter you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then soon after that she left her job and left Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: She took her children with her?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so would it be fair to say that the journalist would not have been able to get that information had -- and was it a man? A woman? Was it several people that spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection, compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who spoke to you, ma'am, that you think is a journalist?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: A man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was it only one person or was there more than one person even if only one was asking questions?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Two other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know if either of those men were, in fact, authorities maybe or police officers investigating crimes in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He introduced himself as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that in 1992 you would have been happy to give a statement against the crimes of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, was it this time before the fighting started that a number of SDS extremists took to the woods and began attacks on Dobrun, Kabernik and Srenicka [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Dobrun, Kabernik and Nezuci.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And on the 10th of April, that's an important date for you in your memory, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the most important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's when your brother came to you and said he was going to join Murat at the dam?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What did your brother tell you that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He said that I should go and that he'll have to -- that Murat would let the dam break. That's all he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, was your house threatened by the water or the flood where it was located or was it on high ground?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: My house was just above the dam on a slight elevation, but there was nothing in our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that they wanted to let the water out of the dam to cut off the bridges that would allow Serbians to go into primarily Muslim territory on the other side of the Drina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Can you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the strategy behind letting the water out of the dam was to break bridges so that Serbians would not be able to across into Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: If she can answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that strategy, Witness? Do you know what was behind that strategy, what was its purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, later on you indicate that one of the bridges was broken on the Drina by the water being let out of the dam; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the bridge was broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were other bridges damaged or broken because of the water being let out of the dam?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at that time you first fled your home and went to Gorazde; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: All of my people went to Gorazde, my father was seriously ill, I stayed in Visegrad therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because he could not travel at that time, your father?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He was very seriously ill and he could not leave the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you recall the date that the Uzice Corps came into town as the 13th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, I cannot remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why can't you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I cannot remember because I wasn't interested. I was never interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, when the Uzice Corps came into town, that was a large amount of troops, armour, and weapons coming into the territory and these troops were of Serbian descent. Wouldn't that cause you concern?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Because when the Uzice Corps was there things were peaceful, no one took anyone away and no one killed anyone; as soon as the Uzice Corps left the slaughter and the killing started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yet your travel during those days that the Uzice Corps was there, your travel was limited to around taking care of your father; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you, in fact, went to Gorazde yourself; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I did not go to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You didn't stay there -- but your family stayed there for how long then?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes. The man asked for a glass of water. I gave him a glass of water and the man said to me - I don't know this man's name, I don't know who he is - he told me that we should run away because our neighbours would slaughter us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that was the first day the Uzice Corps came to your home?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: It was when the Uzice Corps was supposed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And I want to go back to when you first returned or your family first returned from Gorazde, and isn't it true that the Uzice Corps came to your house demanding to know the location of your brother Muho?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: It's not Muho, it's Mujo. Yes, this man came, he's from the Uzice Corps, asking where my brother was and I said I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at that time he told you he knew you were lying; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, even if he did say something you don't have to ask me about everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, isn't it true that he told you he'd had your phone being recorded and had a cassette to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He said that and he left, and -- I mean, do you have any other questions about my brother?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, maybe only a couple, but I was going to move on. I'm going through your earlier statement in March and asking you if these things are true. And so it sounds to me like they are true; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, counsel has just said earlier statement in March. I wonder whether that was an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That was an error. I meant July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, after that they cut off your telephone, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And they came back every day for seven or eight days to intimidate you; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That the Uzice Corps after they cut off your phone and told you they knew you'd been speaking to your brother, they came back every day for seven days?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that probably caused great fear and intimidation in your family; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, nothing is my fault. I'm not to be blamed for anything. Why would I be afraid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That should be true, ma'am, but I'm sure that this brought some fear that harm might befall your family.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: What can be worse? They killed my husband, brother, and father. Can anything be worse in this world?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I don't believe that can be worse, and that's why I'm asking you about what you remember. Now, after -- is it true, though, that they did come for seven days and after that you decided to hide in the woods?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I hid in the woods when Behka Zukic was killed. Until then I never slept in the woods, I slept in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So after the Uzice Corps came for seven days in a row that didn't cause you concern enough to go hide in the woods with your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I answered that very same question to you a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you were in your village and that -- could you please say the name of your village so I don't mispronounce it again.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Dusce is its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in your village you saw soldiers taking Muslims away; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you call them soldiers. How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, they wore military clothing. On their sleeves they had a white eagle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, what is the point you're trying to make with this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm taking her through the events immediately surrounding, of course, early -- late of May and early of June which I think is all relevant time-period for the crimes accused against my client. I think the level of her recollection is important, also the fact that I'm going through a statement of which she says she signed but did not read a typewritten one, I think laying a foundation is important also because if she affirms a lot of the things in this statement that was clearly in July of 1992, then I think clearly it also establishes that that information only could have come from this witness because of the personal nature and the details that could not have been gotten from some other hearsay source.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you say you saw white eagles on their arms. Can you describe this emblem with detail, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Listen to me, sir, can you remember what you ate 16 years ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, ma'am, but my countrymen were not taken away by people wearing white eagles and I'd like to think I would remember what that looked like and I'm asking you if you can recall that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I just remember that they took people away and killed them. You have the list of people who were taken away and who were killed. These people are recorded as missing. No one has ever found them. He has to know where these people of ours are so that at least people would know where their graves are and that they could be buried properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so would it be fair to say that you cannot identify or describe this insignia that was on their arm today for the Court?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I described it once and I'm not going to describe it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, it's a matter of some importance, and counsel has asked you whether you can describe the emblem, the white eagle. Are you in a position to describe it for the benefit of the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give an answer to the Judges but not to the rest of these people. On the sleeve there was something sewn on, this white eagle was sewn on to the sleeve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I know you may be a little upset, Witness, because you have been through a lot but the procedure which we have does entitle counsel to ask questions. If the questions are in any way improper, then I will not permit them to be asked. So I'll ask you to be patient and to answer the questions which are asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, in response to the Judge's question you said eagle was sewn on. Is it eagle or eagles, as in more than one?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Eagle, one eagle, regardless of where it is worn, on a T-shirt, whatever, it is just a sign, an emblem, and how many of them there were with that, that I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that you had only heard later that these soldiers were members of the White Eagles; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: As soon as the Uzice Corps left, these soldiers arrived. Maybe there were there before that but I had never heard of them. As soon as the Uzice Corps left, Behka Zukic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you recollect the date of that -- of an incident at the Zukic home being the 21st of May, 1992; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No, the 18th, before that, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why do you know that the murder of Ms. Zukic occurred on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I know because Behka Zukic wanted to leave when the army was leaving Visegrad. She left with her family. Sredoje Lukic and Milan Lukic returned them home to Dusce. He came the second time, he took away their truck. Milan Lukic on the first occasion took the Passat and the next time Sredoje Lukic took the truck, and he took these people away. I wish we knew at least where the graves of these people are so that they could be buried properly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can barely hear the witness because of background noise and typing. Other microphones are on. Could they please be switched off when she's speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And, ma'am, what time of day did the Serbians first come to the Zukic home?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I cannot answer that. I don't know. I don't know what time of day was. I know that they first came when they took away their Passat, that was the first time. The second time when they came -- well, it's to say during the course of the day. I mean, it had to be before dark fell, it couldn't have been before that because Behka was killed exactly at 12.00 at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What time during the day did they first come --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question. The mike was off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When they first came outside the house and stole the Passat, what time of day was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I don't know what the answer to that question would be, what time of day it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, would it be fair to say that before the day that Ms. Zukic -- the Passat was stolen, you'd never met Milan Lukic before?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I saw him before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when did you see him before this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I saw him before they returned Behka. I saw him when I was coming back from work, I saw Milan Lukic at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What date was this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The 18th, that was the date, at 3.00 I left work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so on the 18th -- and then you say he introduced himself; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, possibly he introduced himself then but I personally do not remember the date when he said that his name was Milan Lukic and that he is 25 and that he came there to slaughter Muslims. Have you got anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, I have a lot more, to be honest with you, because the details in this kind of case are important and you are one of the few people that has come forward to say you have those details in your memory and we do need to exhaust them, please. Can you do that for us?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, on the first day you met Milan Lukic what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Military clothing. In my life I've never seen him in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And as military clothing, what colour?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, that I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I mean, they could be green, they could be black, they could be blue, I guess in imagination they could be any colour but I'm hoping you remember.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you say that Mr. Lukic never wore a cap, so we can't say he had anything on his head; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He had nothing on his head then. Every time I saw him, he never had anything on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What colour was his hair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Oh, it was dark, black, I mean it wasn't too short, it wasn't too long. He had normal hair. His cap was stuck to his blouse. How can I say anything about this? I was never very knowledgeable about this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, you said that you had come very close to him on some occasions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I did get close but I don't remember the date. Milan Lukic, is he going to remember when he was eating cherries on the bridge and when he slaughtered this man and when the corpse fell into the water and when the head remained on the bridge? He should remember that, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you and your Muslim neighbours talked a lot, both before and after the war, about who was responsible?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Before the war I didn't talk about who was responsible for that or after the war. There are authorities who are in charge of that and who should take care of that; it's not us, the ordinary citizens, who should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, would it be fair to say that some of those authorities would be the investigators in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And those would be the proper authorities to give a statement to; wouldn't that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection. It's quite misleading, as it's unclear exactly what investigators counsel is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's misleading. He asked whether it would be fair to say that some of those authorities would be the investigators in Sarajevo. Perhaps you can clarify, Mr. Alarid, with more specificity. What investigators are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I mean, she claims to have given this statement to journalists -- a journalist, yet two other men were in the room that did not say anything. The statement then appears with some facts that I think could only have come from this witness and I think are somewhat reliable. I understand the witness has different recollections 16 years later. However, in light of the fact that it appears on what is regular and official letterhead of Bosnia and Herzegovina, clearly an investigative reporting document in connection with alleged crimes, I think, one, it's regular on its face in terms of authenticity purposes and the fact that she affirmed that she signed it also goes to that. And so I -- I'm assuming that they were investigators considering the fact that, one, the nature of the report is investigative in nature, it appears to serve the purpose of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The witness has not said that she signed this statement. She has said that she signed a handwritten version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you want to say something too?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, to add something. I think that I heard that the witness said that her signature is on that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: However, both in her testimony as well as in her statement from the 26th of August, she says she did not sign a typed version of the statement. She confirms her signature appears there but she does not say she signed the statement. In fact, she says she signed only a handwritten version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And on the transcript, page 44, line 22, I believe is the answer to that question. The question -- my question was: "But regardless, you do identify your signature at the end of the Serbian typewritten statement; is that correct?" And the answer was: "Yes, that's my signature."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, so what is it that you want to do now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, Your Honour, I was doing this foundational kind of back -- going back further than I cared to because the state had objected to the foundational requirements for this earlier statement, which of course we got through the OTP in their disclosure so it's not like we, you know, fabricated this, it came from them. And in fact, we just received the signed statement this last week, of which I wouldn't have even been able to ask that question. I would prefer to introduce the statement, allow the Court to assess the weight of the earlier statement against changes that have obviously subsequently been made in the OTP statement of March -- and that's why I misspoke as to March of 2001, and also she made some corrections on her proofing statements and I think it would be helpful for the Chamber to have all statements when they review the evidence in the final and then I could move on to the more pertinent, factual allegations against Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, introduce the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: At this time we would tender the statements marked as 1D00-3146 -- oh, I guess it wasn't admitted but I did tender, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those statements are already in evidence as Exhibits 1D23 and 1D24.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I guess when the Prosecutor objected, I thought it was still up in the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's already in evidence. What is the question you wish to put now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I can move on, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you did have an opportunity to review this earlier typewritten statement, ma'am, and you again say that you never gave it or signed a typewritten one. But yet you did have an opportunity to review the facts; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say in that statement you indicated that the contact at the Zukic home was in fact on the 21st of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The 18th in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When -- I understand today you're testifying that it was the 18th, but in the earlier statement, which you at least reviewed, it said it was the 21st; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: 21st is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And again I ask you: Would it be fair to say that a person's memory should be better a month or two after an incident as opposed to several years after an incident? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: In 1992 there was still a war going on and I was down there and it's hard to forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so again, your memory should be very clear in July of 1992; wouldn't that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, with regards to the Zukic incident, isn't it true that when the Passat was taken Ms. Zukic was still alive?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that who did that left and then night fell; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The one who did it, Milan Lukic did it, he took his -- took Behka's Passat and drove away. And Sredoje Lukic, in the other vehicle, he drove off in front of their house. Now, was it night-time or not, that I don't know the answer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well -- but wouldn't it be fair to say that it would be really hard to identify people in the dark?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: If it was night-time, well, I saw Milan Lukic when he killed Behka. No one can convince me otherwise, when he killed her personally. If necessary, I can describe it very well for you. I know what Behka was wearing as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: You say that the murder of Ms. Zukic occurred at around midnight?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's exactly when it happened, 12.00. One gun-shot and that killed Behka at 12.00 at night, and he told me that I'd be the next victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was the name of your father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Jakuf Kahriman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that your father-in-law woke you up at 2355 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that your father-in-law woke you up, telling you that they've ripped everything out of Ms. -- out of the Tabakovic house?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Tabakovic, the robbery was the day before, or rather, the day after, not the day before. Behka was killed on the 18th, meaning the Tabakovics got home on the 19th and they started taking all that stuff away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, we're going to take the break now, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, let us move quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: More focused. Time is not indeterminate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I just wanted to say that before we started this witness's testimony the witness made a sincere request to be -- to complete before the weekend so that she could return to her family. I'm merely putting that on the record. I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry you didn't say that before, but we'll do our best, you know. It may not be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And of course, you are aware that we are stopping at 1.15 today? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, going back to the day that Mrs. Zukic was killed, that was late in the afternoon, after midnight; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you didn't see exactly who killed Ms. Zukic because you were not in her house; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I wasn't in her house but I went in when Milan Lukic killed Behija Zukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you actually saw the trigger being pulled is what you're saying today?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I didn't see the trigger being pulled. I just saw Milan Lukic hold a rifle, and he held his trigger at the switch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that in order to get into the home of Ms. Zukic, Huso Jamak had to kick in the door?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that the assailants of Ms. Zukic on that night left in a white car?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No, not in a white car. The people were taken away in a lorry, in a white car, and when Milan killed Behka he left in her Passat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you have used 44 minutes. I am not expecting that you will be taking up the rest of the time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how much time longer do I have, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would say another 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at what time did Ms. Zukic's daughter arrive at the scene?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: She arrived, I can't remember when exactly. The morning we came, I covered Behka's body and the daughter cried and she said, My mom has been killed. And I said, No, that's not true. I didn't have the courage to face up to them and tell them that their mother had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that is when Huso Jamak, who is her daughter's uncle, was there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, he was and he left - what shall I call that? - I'm not sure what you call that here, some sort of an ambulance. He went to a hospital. Some doctor came and Behka was taken away immediately in that car.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, wasn't Omer Omerovic there as well and --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Omer Omerovic was taken away. Omer Omerovic could not possibly have been there because he lives not a huge distance from Behka's place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Uzeir Imamovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Imamovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I used to know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that it was them that went off to get a doctor and order the ambulance, not Huso.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Huso himself went away to call the doctor, Huso Jamak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the names of Omer and Uzeir would not have been available to the investigators or journalists in Sarajevo had you not mentioned their names?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, after this incident you relocated to the home of Remzo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that was also with your husband?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that on that next day at 1.00 in the afternoon the Chetniks had come to the home looking for Remzo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And they searched the home?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And tell me about the Chetnik leader Buko?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: His name was Buco, not Buko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I apologise, ma'am, it's my pronunciation in reading this. Tell me about Buco.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, he came, he took my gold and jewellery away, he took everything that I had on me, my money, and then he told me if I ever went to see the police about that, they'd be back to kill me and my kids.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he also came back the next day and robbed you again?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He came back and he wanted my earrings, the ones that I was actually wearing. There was a man who was there with him and he said, What about what the lady gave you last night, you find that not to be enough or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then a little later you saw four Chetniks pass by in a passenger car and stop at the Kustura house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And they took Hasib Murtic red Fiat?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this was all the next day after Ms. Zukic was killed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then three men -- or excuse me, four men went into the home including Hasib and only three men came out; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And after -- on the second day after their arrival you decided to go into the home; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's when you found Mr. Murtic killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I'm wondering about the relevance of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, what's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The relevance is that this is all the time-period concerning issues surrounding the allegations of -- against my client, Milan Lukic. I believe that there are material changes between earlier statements and the most recent statements, including the proofing statement. I think we need to go through, explore her recollection, because it appears that some of the original 1992 were very, very correct in terms of this witness's recollection of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you are coming to the discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, do so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And at no time do you identify who you thought was Milan Lukic as part of this particular situation?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I didn't identify him when he came to Murtic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And there was a man that was killed, Safet Omerovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When was he killed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you indicated earlier or would it be true that the criminals who killed him were Serbs, our neighbours, wearing stockings over their faces?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then would it be fair to say that during this time-period the Chetniks continued to loot Muslim houses in Dusce?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this continued until the 10th of June, 1992, when you saw two Chetniks go into the Varda company?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that they removed a total of five workers from the Varda factory and two from the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the seven workers were taken out by the two Chetniks to the Drina -- the bridge over the Drina which had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: It was under the bridge that the people were killed. I'm not sure who described it that way. It was under the bridge, wasn't it, maybe 1 or 3 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how far away from you [sic] were you when you saw this killing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: 2 kilometres away, when Milan Lukic brought those people there. He told them to get into the river and he shot them from behind, but I didn't recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you didn't recognise the workers but you recognised Mr. Milan Lukic from 2 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true, though, that the Chetniks that committed that killing got into a blue car?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the Chetniks that committed this crime had unusually large kokarda on their caps?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't really say. Mitar Vasiljevic wore a hat and he had a huge kokarda displayed on that hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That was a cowboy hat?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, black.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you remember the 10th of June so well because, of course, that was the day your husband was killed or you at least found out that he was killed; isn't that true, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I remember that my was killed on the 10th of June, 1992, at Osojnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that is where you know the people to have done this were Slobodan Tripkovic and Ranko; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And Slobodan Tripkovic carried a sniper rifle; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you otherwise describe him besides the sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I have nothing to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the last word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just repeat what you said, Witness. Can you repeat the answer you gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't describe that man. He had a sniper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Alarid, you have about seven minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Be sure that you utilise the time efficiently. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I submit that the line of questioning with regard to the Varda incident that we just passed from was misleading to the witness because the question -- the first question on that was the 10th of June when you saw the Chetniks go to the Varda factory. And then when he asked about the killing she said: "I can't remember that." Then counsel proceeded to ask her about this killing. Now, the witness does speak about an incident that she observed at the Varda factory which was a killing but she offers a different date. So I submit that this is somewhat misleading and that that issue should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the different date that is being referred to was not testified by the witness but is otherwise in her inconsistent statements which have been also tendered into evidence. I think it would be for the Court to assess the weight of those statements against each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, would it be fair to say that you were not able to bury your husband?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I wasn't able to do that. They didn't hand over my husband's body for me to bury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you're drowning us in a sea of fairness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, it's a bad habit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you testified that, in fact, in Ms. Zukic's home you spoke with Milan Lukic specifically and he told you to get out of his way; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: He didn't tell me to get out of the way. He just said I'd be the next victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Don't you think it's illogical that he would allow you to live at that point in time if he was willing to kill another Muslim woman?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Why didn't he just kill me right there and then? I guess you'd have to ask him about that, why he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that the date you left on the buses from the -- in front of the Visegrad Hotel was June 15th?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The 14th, that's when I saw Milan Lukic; on the 15th, we left Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that's what I asked you, isn't it true that on the bus it was June 15th; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The 15th of June outside the hotel in Visegrad, that's where we left from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. Cepic, how long will you be?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Half an hour roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And will there be any re-direct -- sorry, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that the night before you left on the bus you spent the night with a colleague, Jasmina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you remember the night before you left on the bus where you spent the night?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I spent it somewhere in the town, but I don't remember where exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know Jasmina, do you remember her?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Does she live in -- do you know the Vucine residential area? Would that --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: It's a neighbourhood, that was where I spent the night, in Vucine, but I can't remember at whose place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it true that Jasmina lives in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: She lived somewhere or other, I'm not sure where and I'm not sure where I spent that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you know a Ferid Spahic, Zuco?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Zuco, yes, I know him, they called him Zuco. About Ferid, I never knew his real name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was Zuco on the bus with you that was later separated --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No, no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about Mr. Spahic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But at the very least, you're certain you were on the bus on the 15th; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I apologise. Why are you so certain about the 15th?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I'm certain and I can swear upon it, on the 15th of June, 1992, that's when we left Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you have exhausted the time allotted to you. It is now the turn of Mr. Cepic to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could look me in the eye so I can introduce myself. I'm Djuro Cepic. I'm here on behalf of Mr. Sredoje Lukic. I will be asking you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you scroll down this statement, please. A little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we see in the lower corner at the bottom of the page, that's your signature, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And then the speakers overlap and the interpreter didn't get that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You provided a physical description of my client today, Mr. Sredoje Lukic. You say --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the witness's answer was cut off and then never clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What was the answer? There's no answer. The -- you were asked the question, Witness, that you provided a physical description of Mr. Sredoje Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I'm talking about the question before, where the witness was asked: "... that's your signature, right?" And the witness said: "... that's my signature, but," and then the interpreter said the speakers overlapped so he didn't get the last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will you finish that answer for us, Witness, in relation to your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my signature, but it wasn't written like this. It was a handwritten statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the interests of time -- short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, we got this statement from the OTP, we got it as your statement and as a statement that was authentic. Are you trying to tell us that the state authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the OTP are using a document that is ill-founded? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: What I'm saying is it wasn't written like this. The journalist introduced himself and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about after the 1992 statement, up until 2001 when you provide another statement to the investigators of the OTP -- between these two statements did you provide any other statements to any of the appropriate authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the public prosecutor, anyone like that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Does that not strike you as slightly illogical? It had been a long time after all. You are a witness. You are also an injured party. You are a victim. Doesn't that strike you as slightly illogical?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course you know about the 1992 statement. You signed each and every page of that statement. No reference to my client's name, Sredoje Lukic, whatsoever, you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't quite remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did it happen that you gave this statement in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I gave a statement to The Hague Tribunal in 2001 in my country, in the country in which I currently reside. Can you please re-ask that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who got in touch with you about that statement and who mediated?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't remember the name of the man back in 2001. It was a Hague investigator and he wanted me to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who had given him your phone number?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: That's not something that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You tell us today that you used to see Sredoje Lukic three times a day on the streets of Visegrad. In your statement dated 2001, you described him in the following terms, a man somewhat shorter than Milan Lukic and you didn't know what his job was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What sort of clothes was he wearing at the time you used to see him three times a day, rather sporty or maybe a black tie?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Now, this is something that I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sporting a moustache, a beard perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you something, sir, if you think back to that time, could you possibly remember if he wore a moustache or a beard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just answer the questions asked by counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You told us today that you used to see him three times a day.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yet you can't remember this type of detail? That's what you're telling us today, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, I can't remember that type of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit number P33 on our screens and paragraph 28, please. This is page -- I think fifth page in English and in B/C/S it should be also fifth. The statement of this witness from 2001, 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, we're waiting for this to come up on our screens but let's try to cover some ground before that happens. You describe a rather serious incident in Visegrad that occurred sometime in -- late in May 1992. In the square outside the Visegrad Hotel a local, an ethnic Croat, was impaled, his name was Slavko?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let me see if I can jog your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, thank you. And could we have also in B/C/S -- yes, it has to be the fifth page. Could we have on second part of our screens in English also, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this turns up, I mean before the English comes up, can you please read paragraph 2. It reads: "One of the last days of May 1992 ..."

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: "One of the last days of May 1992, I saw that a local of Croat ethnicity had been impaled on the square in front of Visegrad Hotel. His name was Slavko and I didn't know his last name. He was a lab technician taking blood samples at the hospital ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement, Madam?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: It is my statement. Some bits appear to have been added -- not the entire statement is mine and I'm referring to the Bosnian over here, the statement I gave to the OTP investigators -- I agree with that statement in every respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is your statement to the OTP investigators in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Okay, that's right, I gave a statement, but again I'm telling you I can't quite remember, can I.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have -- could we scroll down in English this page just to check the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, are these your initials over here, did you sign this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, can we conclude that what is written in this statement does not reflect what it was that you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Again, I'm telling you I can't remember that day, but I do know that Sredoje Lukic killed a man and impaled him. Now, what day that happened I really cannot remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, let's have a look at this. This Slavko, this lab technician who took blood samples in the hospital --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You knew him?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I knew the man personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: He was 50-something at that point when he was killed; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I don't know how old he was. I can't say exactly what his age was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That was the only man in the lab of the Visegrad medical centre; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: There were several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But he was the only Slavko?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No, he was not the only Slavko. There were several men who worked at the lab in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, could you describe to us where it was that you stood on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you really want to know, I stood in front of the department store in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How many people were there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, they were all there and Sredoje Lukic was among them, and as for us civilians there weren't that many of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you give us some details about this Slavko. What did he look like? How old was he? What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm telling you yet again, I cannot remember how old he was and what he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, what kind of a day was this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, that I really don't know, what kind of a day it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Where was the impaling rod?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: If you really want to know, it was on the square by the street that used to be called Marsal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who else was there in addition to yourself, as far as civilians were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No one, just me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago you said that there were several of you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I said several of us, but I mean it's not sort of like normal citizens wearing normal clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, since you say that you knew this Slavko --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Why would I agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let me just say what I have to say. That Slavko Tomic then was 50-something, that he was the only man who was a lab technician, and the only one who took blood samples at the hospital and the only Slavko, over several decades at that, who worked at the Visegrad hospital and whose name was Slavko. You have to agree with me on that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you on that because several people worked in Visegrad taking blood samples, it wasn't only Slavko.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Give us a specific detail so that we would distinguish between this Slavko and some other Slavko.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I'm telling you yet again, sir, I don't know what the man's last name was. He was an ethnic Croat, this man was, the only Croat living in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you once again whether you remember how old he was and what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I do not remember how old he was and I don't remember what the man looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, can you give us some more information that would throw more light on this grave incident in relation to Slavko or in relation to anything else? You say here that you knew him very well?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I knew the man but I'm telling you, I cannot remember what it was that the man was wearing and what he was like. I mean, I cannot remember that picture. There was one Slavko who was a Serb and there was one Slavko who was a Croat, sir, if you really want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How old was the one who was the victim roughly?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I told you very nicely, I don't know how old the man was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My learned friend is on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this question has been asked and answered numerous times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, move on, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, would you be surprised if I were to tell you that I carried out an investigation on the basis of this statement of yours and that in the history of the Visegrad medical centre there was just one Slavko who had worked there over a span of several decades -- let me finish, please. And that there was only one man, precisely this Slavko, who worked in the lab. And would you be surprised if I were to tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us not prompt the objection, compound question. Would you be surprised to hear that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. What's the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, would you be surprised - and it is with pleasure that I call upon my friends of the Prosecution to carry out an investigation in relation to these assertions - that this Slavko was the only lab technician in the history of the medical centre of Visegrad is alive until this day and he still lives in Visegrad --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: This appears to me to be again the same question put to the witness repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I put my next question, in relation to this alleged incident it is with pleasure that I call upon my colleagues from the Prosecution, I'm going to give them all the necessary references and let them investigate this incident if there's any doubt in their minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. They would have heard you. I'm not sure that's the proper medium, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, just two more questions. When you gave your first statement you knew that Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic was on trial; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the counsel please clarify when he says "first statement" so the witness will clearly understand which statement he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What statement is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The first statement to the OTP in 2001, the OTP of The Hague Tribunal, you knew then that Mitar Vasiljevic was on trial? Please go ahead. I do apologise, Madam, have you heard my question?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear it. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. When you made your statement to The Hague investigators in 2001, you knew that proceedings against Mitar Vasiljevic were underway; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you a member of the Association of Women War Victims?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 54th paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, along with your statement we received a page from a photo album where you drew a circle around --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise. This is Exhibit number P -- the same statement, just a couple of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- paragraphs further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S is the -- just one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Maybe I could assist. Paragraph 54 in the English is the second-to-last paragraph of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Eighth page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you said under oath that you looked at three series of photographs and that in one of them you recognised Momir Savic. Do you see that here? Do you see what it says on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I recognised Momir Savic. If necessary, I'll recognise him yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you another question now. Three photo albums were shown to you, or rather, three photo-spreads, three pages with pictures -- allow me to finish, please --

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: How can I remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Allow me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It seems to me that counsel is misstating the B/C/S version of the witness's statement. The first time he posed the question I believe he used the words of her statement which say "tri niza," which is three rows. The second time he put the statement he said three pages. I might be mistaken. I just want to make sure that we're very clear on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, what is the question that you put?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Discrepancy, discrepancy, Your Honour, just if you allow me. This is a wrong translation. Three photo-spreads, three photo-spreads, it is shown to the witness and witness signed this statement in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you signed a statement under oath to the effect that you were shown three photo-spreads; however, today you stated something different. You changed your statement and you said that you had only one sheet in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I just had this one sheet in front of me and I recognised Momir Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just final question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. -- again -- remember, you want this lady to leave, so what is your objection this time?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Simply a question that there may be a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And the translation problem is not the witness's error but rather a translation error.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Should we have to explore everything in signatures and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have about two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I already finished but I just have to raise that issue regarding to that objection which is this is the OTP statement, it is not some other statement. This is from your -- your office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And huge discrepancy -- the problem is, Your Honour -- but I will raise that issue as preliminary issue. The problem is -- and it was about photo-spreads, missing photo-spreads. We raised that issue for a couple times during the pre-trial phase and now we have a clear evidence that witness is changing their testimony in relation to those photo-spreads. Also related to VG-97, it was also marked in his statement that it was shown to him one photo-spread, we did not find that photo-spread also. This is the second problem up to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber notes the submissions that you have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just final question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, how come this change in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: There is no change in my statement. If necessary --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I was trying to do my best to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much and the Chamber is in appreciation of your efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, on the night that Behija Zukic was killed, how did you get into her house?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I went across the terrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How long after the shots were fired would you say you went into her house?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Well, as soon as I saw the shot, I entered the house; that is to say, Milan and Sredoje could not have left immediately. Milan was holding the trigger on the rifle, whereas Sredoje's rifle was on his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, you described in your statement, your March 2001 statement to the Tribunal, you described a killing that you observed at the Varda factory. Could you clarify, please, if you recall on what date you observed that killing?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Apart from the 25th of May, 1992, incident, did you observe any other incidents in relation to the Varda factory?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, when you were interviewed by a journalist in July 1992, how many people were present at that interview?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: There were two other men along with the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were they introduced to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did they give you any reason to believe that they were part of any authority structure?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: It never could have crossed my mind because he introduced himself as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The statement that you gave to that journalist on that day, was it read back to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you read it before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was it typed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No, no, handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In 1992, did you ever sign a typed statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Have you ever given a statement to the police in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: For the last question could I please ask the court officer to call up the witness's statement from 2001, it's the one we just had on our screen. I think it's P34, Exhibit P34, I believe, her 2001 statement, and could we please kindly return to that second-to-last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Ms. Kahriman, can you see -- sorry, I'm just waiting for the text to appear on the screen. Can you see the paragraph in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Would you be so kind, please, as to read the first line.

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: The first one or the second one?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The very first line, it begins with "pokazana."

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: "Three series of photographs were shown to me and I was asked whether I recognised any one of the photographs. From one of the series I recognised the photograph of Momir Savic, number 2, I signed the photograph and I wrote the name" -- the date.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether this was one page of photographs or two or three pages of photographs? How many pages of photographs were you shown?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was this one photograph shown, as far as I can remember, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So just to clarify, is this one piece of paper or more than one piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MIRSADA KAHRIMAN
utterances.text: It was one piece of paper; however, there were several photographs on that one piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, that concludes your evidence, and you may now leave. We will adjourn and resume on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 1st day of September, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Private session] [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of Chamber]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.13 p.m.,
